summary.text: Counting pairs divisible by each power \(p^i\) gives numerator valuation \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor^2\), while Legendre’s formula gives denominator valuation \(\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r\le \lfloor N/p^i\rfloor} r\lfloor\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor/r\rfloor\); the latter is at most the former termwise, so the quotient is integral. For \(N=np+k\) with \(k<p\), every \(\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor\) for \(i\ge1\) equals \(\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\), making their valuation difference independent of \(k\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 U(N)=\prod_{j=1}^N\prod_{r=1}^N \gcd(j,r),
 \qquad
 D(N)=\prod_{r=1}^N\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nr\right\rfloor!\right)^r.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
 a(N)=\frac{U(N)}{D(N)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and obtain formulas for all of its prime valuations. We then show directly from those formulas that its valuation at a given prime is constant on every block
\(np,np+1,\ldots,np+p-1\).

Throughout, for a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in \(x\).

### 1. The valuation of the numerator

Fix a prime \(q\), an integer \(N\geq 0\), and an integer \(B>N\). We claim that
\[
 v_q(U(N))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
 \tag{1}
\]

For positive integers \(j,r\),
\[
 v_q(\gcd(j,r))=\min(v_q(j),v_q(r)).
\]
Moreover, this minimum can be counted one power of \(q\) at a time:
\[
 \min(v_q(j),v_q(r))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}.
 \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, for each \(i\geq1\), both divisibilities hold exactly when
\(i\leq \min(v_q(j),v_q(r))\). The upper cutoff \(B-1\) loses nothing: since
\(1\leq j,r\leq N<B\), neither valuation can reach \(B\).

Taking valuations of the product defining \(U(N)\), using (2), and interchanging the finite sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_q(U(N))
 &=\sum_{j=1}^N\sum_{r=1}^N v_q(\gcd(j,r))\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
   \left(\sum_{j=1}^N{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}\right)
   \left(\sum_{r=1}^N{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
There are exactly \(\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) among
\(1,\ldots,N\). This proves (1).

### 2. The valuation of the denominator

Under the same assumptions, we claim
\[
 v_q(D(N))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\sum_{r=1}^N
 r\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i r}\right\rfloor
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\sum_{r=1}^N
 r\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor}{r}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{3}
\]

For any nonnegative integer \(m\), counting the factors divisible by each successive power of \(q\) in \(m!\) gives Legendre's formula
\[
 v_q(m!)=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Apply this with \(m=\lfloor N/r\rfloor\). Since valuation multiplies by \(r\) on taking an \(r\)-th power,
\[
 v_q(D(N))
 =\sum_{r=1}^N r\sum_{i\geq1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.

tag{4}
\]
Successive integer division obeys
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N}{rq^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/q^i\rfloor}{r}\right\rfloor.
\]
Also, terms with \(i\geq B\) vanish because \(q^i>N\) (a prime is at least 2, so \(q^i\geq i+1>B>N\)). Thus (4) is precisely (3).

It will be useful to introduce
\[
 F_L(M)=\sum_{r=1}^L r\left\lfloor\frac Mr\right\rfloor.
\]
Whenever \(M\leq L\), all terms with \(r>M\) vanish, and consequently
\[
 F_L(M)=F_M(M).
 \tag{5}
\]
In this notation, formula (3) says
\[
 v_q(D(N))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}F_N\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor\right).
 \tag{6}
\]

### 3. The quotient is an integer

We next show that \(D(N)\mid U(N)\). Both products are positive (with the usual value 1 for an empty product), so it suffices to compare their valuations at every prime \(q\).

Use (1) and (3), for example with \(B=N+1\), and put
\[
 M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
By (5), the contribution to the denominator valuation for a fixed \(i\) is
\[
 F_N(M_i)=F_{M_i}(M_i)
 =\sum_{r=1}^{M_i}r\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{r}\right\rfloor.
	ag{7}
\]
For every positive \(r\),
\[
 r\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{r}\right\rfloor\leq M_i.
\]
There are \(M_i\) terms in (7), so
\[
 F_N(M_i)\leq M_i^2.
	ag{8}
\]
But \(M_i^2\) is exactly the fixed-\(i\) contribution to the numerator valuation in (1). Summing (8) over \(i\) yields
\[
 v_q(D(N))\leq v_q(U(N))
\]
for every prime \(q\). Hence \(D(N)\mid U(N)\), proving in particular that \(a(N)\) is an integer. Exact division therefore gives
\[
 v_q(a(N))=v_q(U(N))-v_q(D(N)).
 \tag{9}
\]

Combining (1), (6), and (9), for any \(B>N\) we have the useful explicit expression
\[
 v_q(a(N))=
 \sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
 \left[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2
 -F_N\left(\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q^i}\right\rfloor\right)
 \right].
 \tag{10}
\]
The expression as a whole is nonnegative by the preceding divisibility argument; equivalently, each bracket is nonnegative by (8).

### 4. Constancy on a block of length \(p\)

Now let \(n>0\), let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy
\(0\leq k<p\). Set
\[
 N_0=np,\qquad N_1=np+k,
\]
and choose the common cutoff
\[
 B=np+p.
\]
Because \(k<p\), both \(N_0<B\) and \(N_1<B\), so all the preceding valuation formulas may be used with this same cutoff.

The key observation is that, for every \(i\geq1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N_1}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{11}
\]
To see this, first divide by \(p\). Euclidean division and \(0\leq k<p\) give
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor.
	ag{12}
\]
For \(i\geq1\), dividing by \(p^i=p\,p^{i-1}\) can be done successively. Therefore both sides of (11) equal
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor.
	ag{13}
\]
Write this common value as \(M_i\).

Formula (1), with \(q=p\), immediately shows from (11) that
\[
 v_p(U(N_0))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}M_i^2
 =v_p(U(N_1)).
 \tag{14}
\]

For the denominator, formula (6) gives
\[
 v_p(D(N_0))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}F_{N_0}(M_i),
 \qquad
 v_p(D(N_1))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}F_{N_1}(M_i).
	ag{15}
\]
For each \(i\), \(M_i=\lfloor N_0/p^i\rfloor\leq N_0\leq N_1\). Hence the support identity (5) applies twice:
\[
 F_{N_0}(M_i)=F_{M_i}(M_i)=F_{N_1}(M_i).
	ag{16}
\]
Summing (16) in (15) proves
\[
 v_p(D(N_0))=v_p(D(N_1)).
 \tag{17}
\]

Finally, use exact division as in (9). Equations (14) and (17) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p(a(np))
 &=v_p(U(N_0))-v_p(D(N_0))\\
 &=v_p(U(N_1))-v_p(D(N_1))\\
 &=v_p(a(np+k)).
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every \(k\) with \(0\leq k<p\). Thus
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))=
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))=\cdots=
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as claimed.
